title: Quiz: What is a Stochastic Process?

questions.text: A researcher tracks whether a patient is in remission or relapse every month for two years. What type of stochastic process is this?
questions.explanation: The parameter space is discrete (monthly checkups — T = {0, 1, 2, ...} months) and the state space is discrete (remission vs relapse — S = {Remission, Relapse}). This makes it a Type I discrete-time, discrete-state process.

questions.text: In the notation {X(t), t ∈ T}, the parameter space T is:
options: The set of all possible states the process can take
The index set — usually time — over which the process is defined
The probability distribution of X at each time point
questions.explanation: T is the parameter space (index set). It is the set of values that the index t ranges over — most often representing time. The set of values X(t) can take is the state space S, not T.

questions.text: In the notation {X(t), t ∈ T}, the symbol X(t) at a specific time t represents a single fixed number.
questions.explanation: X(t) is a random variable, not a fixed number. Before the outcome is observed, X(t) could take any value in the state space S with various probabilities. Only after the process is realised do we observe a specific value x(t) (lowercase). The collection of all realisations is called a sample path.

questions.text: The number of active COVID-19 cases in a hospital ward, monitored at any point in continuous time, is an example of:
questions.explanation: The number of active cases is always an integer (0, 1, 2, ... — a discrete state space), but it can change at any instant in continuous time when a patient is admitted or discharged. This is a Type II continuous-time, discrete-state process.

questions.text: A deterministic model is always sufficient when we want to predict the long-run average behaviour of a biological system.
questions.explanation: A deterministic model can capture the mean trajectory, but it completely misses variability and rare but important events. Near critical thresholds — such as when a population is small and close to extinction — stochastic fluctuations dominate. For instance, a bacterial colony with expected size 2 has a substantial probability of dying out even though the deterministic model predicts stable persistence. Randomness is intrinsic, not just noise.
